headline: Congress Introduces New 'Deal with It' Pictogram, Hits New Legislative Low
deck: As crises loom large, lawmakers shrug with style while the nation waits.
article:
In a landmark decision amidst a legislative quagmire spanning over ten months, the United States Congress has unanimously approved a new pictogram representing the phrase 'Deal with It.' The pictogram, featuring a cartoonish figure nonchalantly shrugging while clutching a briefcase overflowing with legal documents, is set to redefine communication between government and citizens, albeit without addressing pressing issues like unemployment or climate change.

Congressional aides report an exhaustive 300 hours of design work, with contentious debates over the precise shading of the figure's shoulders and the optimal angle of the briefcase. "The nuances in shading signify our resilience in the face of adversity," remarked Representative Clara P. Grumble, lead sponsor of the proposal, visibly proud of the artwork while veterans of the House expressed envy at its timeless ambiguity.

Starting next week, the pictogram will adorn every federal document, and agencies will be mandated to include it in all responses to citizen inquiries. This decision is part of the 'Effort to Simplify Complexity' initiative, which aims to tackle citizens’ concerns without actually engaging with them. Local residents, however, have their doubts. "I just hope they don't replace my Social Security checks with doodles," said one concerned retiree from Nowhereville, Idaho.

As the nation prepares to embrace its newest emblem of disengagement, experts predict this development will lead to a dramatic uptick in citizens enthusiastically throwing their hands up in the air, both literally and figuratively. While Congress continues to produce more graphics than solutions, one can only wonder: in a world rife with complexity, is a pictogram really what we need?
author: Jordan P. Quill, Legislative Correspondent

oped.title: Pictograms and Pomp: A Masterstroke of Congressional Genius
oped.author: D. I. White, Chief Arbiter of Absurdity
oped.body: Ah, the illustrious Congress, proving once again that when it comes to governance, style truly trumps substance! The new 'Deal with It' pictogram is a masterpiece of modern legislative art—a flickering light in an abyss of incompetence. Critics may howl that our lawmakers have reached a new low, but I posit that it's the citizens' hats that are the true culprits! A nation wearing oversized sombreros and feathery fascinators in the face of crisis deserves nothing less than flippant artistry. May I suggest a bold amendment requiring the public to don even more impractical headwear during legislative sessions? Perhaps a top hat paired with a Hawaiian shirt would inspire Congress to take themselves seriously. Alas, until then, let us bask in the whimsical dereliction of duty, one pictogram at a time. Cheers to Congress for its dazzling distraction!

stories.headline: Local Attorney Launches Pictogram-Based Billing System, Hopes to Collect From Clueless Clients
stories.deck: Visual confusion is now a legally binding contract.
stories.article:
In a groundbreaking move, local attorney Gregor Doodle announced today that he will transition to a pictogram-based billing system, replacing confusing legal jargon with colorful drawings of cats and coffee cups. Clients, who previously struggled to decipher their bills, are now left with the delightful challenge of figuring out why a stick figure on a unicycle costs them two thousand pictograms.

Doodle insists this is not a money grab but rather an artful method to engage clients with their legal fees. "We all know that the more confused they are, the more they’ll pay, right?" he quipped during his press conference, while attempting to recreate the image of a disputed parking ticket with interpretive mime gestures.

stories.headline: New County Fair Introduces Pictogram Pie-Eating Contest, Participants Failing to Digest Rules
stories.deck: Contestants feasted on confusion before eating actual pie.
stories.article:
The annual Grover County Fair proudly announced its latest attraction: a pictogram pie-eating contest, where competitors are tasked with consuming blueberry pies while interpreting complex visual instructions. Unsurprisingly, most participants mistook the diagram of a running dog for a pie, leading to an unprecedented number of canine entries, all of whom seemed eager to partake in the chaos.

Organizers commented that while the event was a spectacular failure in terms of pie consumption, it fostered community spirit as bewildered onlookers united in laughter and befuddlement. "Who knew abstract art of canine appetites could be more appealing than dessert?" asked one fairgoer, clutching his stomach after hours of hysterical laughter.
